source.title: Transformers Learn Two Competing Sorting Algorithms, and Only One Length-Generalizes
source.authors: Khashayar Gatmiry; Nathan W. Henry; C. Su; Emmanuel Abbé; Samy Bengio; Melanie Weber; Jonathan A. Kelner; Peter L. Bartlett

record.tranche_reason: The study finds that models trained on the same task can learn distinct solution types, challenging the claim that they converge to the same algorithm.
record.gate_note: The paper studies sorting and related algorithmic tasks, not grokking as defined in V1: it does not track test accuracy over training time after training accuracy saturates, or test whether smaller training sets increase a grokking delay. It also does not track gradual circuit formation or removal of memorizing components over training. Its initialization experiments measure which solution type emerges and length-generalization, not grokking-like delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data.
record.test_reason: The study trains many seeds of the same architecture on the same task and finds two or more mechanistically distinct solution classes. Which class emerges depends on the initialization seed, the relative initialization scale, vocabulary size, width, depth and task. This bears directly on V6 and argues against it. It is not a grokking study: there is no train/test split (online sampling), training accuracy saturates early, and no delayed test-accuracy jump is tracked. So only V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that two-layer transformers trained on a task one layer can solve converge, depending on initialization, to mechanistically distinct single-stage or two-stage solutions. The solution type can be steered by the relative layer init scale. Which type length-generalizes is task-dependent: two-stage for sorting, single-stage for minimum-finding. So simplicity alone does not predict OOD behaviour. They also propose a gap-specialization and first-layer 'hinting' mechanism for the two-stage sorting solution.
record.recipe_differences: Studies sorting and related tasks with two-layer transformers, online sequence sampling, and length-generalization and ablation measurements; it does not use the grokking setup of modular arithmetic or measure delayed test-accuracy improvement during training.
record.method_sensitivity: Solution type varies with relative initialization scale, vocabulary size, embedding dimension, depth, task, and training length; the relationship between solution type and length-generalization differs across tasks.
record.problems: The paper operationalizes solution type through attention-layer ablation rather than a formal algorithm-identity test. Several mechanistic and accuracy results are reported in figures; the text does not provide exact values for every plotted condition. Its experiments concern small algorithmic tasks, not realistic large-model training.
record.rows_left_out: The gap-wise specialization, hijacking, attention-score, candidate-set, and residual-stream analyses were not included as rows because they do not measure training-time grokking, the versions' named progress measures, or convergence to the same algorithm beyond the solution-type evidence already recorded.

untested.parts: No delayed generalization: online training without a train/test split, no training-set-size manipulation, no test-accuracy jump after saturation.
No training-time trajectory of circuit formation, memorization removal or progress measures. The mechanistic analyses are on final checkpoints.
No non-algorithmic data and no switching of a grokking delay via init scale or weight norm. Init scale steers solution type, not delay.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
No weight-decay or low-norm efficiency test, no critical dataset size, no ungrokking.

Modular arithmetic (the grokking task) is not studied. Only sorting, minimum-finding and greedy coin denomination with small one-head transformers are tested. Algorithm identity is defined operationally by layer ablation.
No optimizer or floating-point artifact analysis.

missing.what: Absolute (symmetric) init scale changes the two-stage share: roughly 50/50 at very small sigma, nearly all single-stage at large sigma, unpredictable in between.
Training length changes the two-stage share non-monotonically (50 seeds per K).

Multi-head models: 67/100 seeds have a removable second layer (2x1 head, d=64) and 5/20 at 2x2 heads. Heads within a used layer are never removable (0/20, 0/15). With two heads all models are single-stage yet length-generalize.

Heterogeneity within the two-stage class. At gap 1, 17 seeds keep above 95% accuracy without attention 2 while 4 fall below 30%. Only 12/17 two-stage checkpoints follow the clean residual pipeline; 5 deviate.
Four-layer length-generalization: only solutions using at least two layers length-generalize (50/50 and 34/50 still sort at length 128).

record.verdict_notes: This is not a grokking study. Training is online with no train/test split, and training accuracy saturates early, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested. It is relevant only to V6, which it challenges in a non-modular-arithmetic setting, citing Clock/Pizza (Zhong et al.) as precedent. The row states were recorded as 'observed', meaning the paper's finding appears; relative to V6's 'same algorithm' claim they should be 'reversed'. The figures conflict slightly: 14 versus 16 one-layer four-layer models.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure test accuracy over training time after training accuracy saturates, nor the effect of training-set size on a delay.
Mechanistic analyses are not a training-time trajectory; gradual circuit formation, later removal of memorizing components, and anticipation of an accuracy jump are not tested.
The tasks are algorithmic, and initialization changes are not tested for switching grokking-like delays on or off. Non-algorithmic data and weight-norm/lazy-to-rich effects are not tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
The study does not test weight decay or another low-norm bias as an efficiency account, nor a critical dataset size or ungrokking.

Tests sorting and two related algorithmic tasks in the reported architectures and settings; it does not establish the range of tasks and architectures on which distinct algorithms occur. Solution type is identified operationally by attention-layer ablation, not by a formal proof of algorithm identity.
Does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts as an explanation for grokking.

rows.subject: Two-layer sorting transformers, single-stage seeds (aggregate)

rows.baseline: Full model retains perfect sorting accuracy
rows.value: Full sample accuracy retained; the second attention is ablatable without impacting accuracy
rows.note: Aggregate result for seeds classified as single-stage; the paper describes their ablated accuracy as 100%.
rows.check: Taken with r2, this shows a split across seeds in second-attention removability (removability is 1 for single-stage seeds). Relative to V6's 'same algorithm', the state should be reversed, not observed. On its own the row shows only one class.

relationships.condition: Two-layer one-head sorting transformers, same task and symmetric init, varying only seed
relationships.reason: Second-attention ablation splits seeds into two classes (r1, r2), 26% two-stage at symmetric init (r6), and the classes differ in length-generalization (r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: Second-attention ablation separated seeds into two solution classes with different length generalization, and 26% used the two-stage solution under symmetric initialization.

source_check.condition: Two-layer one-head sorting transformers, same task and symmetric init, varying only seed
source_check.reason: r1/r2 show distinct ablation-defined classes under the same configuration; r4/r5 show different generalization, and r6 reports a mixed seed distribution.

relationships.condition: Sorting models varying relative init scale, vocabulary size, embedding width and depth
relationships.reason: The emerging solution type shifts from 0% to 100% two-stage with small init changes (r7, r8, r14), vocabulary (r9, r10) and width (r11, r12). Four-layer models show several layer-count classes (r13).
relationships.display_finding: Initialization, vocabulary and width changes shifted two-stage solution prevalence from 0% to 100%, while four-layer models exhibited several classes distinguished by the number of layers used.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Sorting models varying relative init scale, vocabulary size, embedding width and depth
source_check.reason: r7–r14 show solution selection changing with initialization, task dimensions and depth, contrary to unrestricted algorithm invariance.

relationships.condition: Strongly asymmetric init or extreme width (sigma2=0.013, sigma1=0.012, E=32, E=80)
relationships.reason: Within these conditions nearly all seeds converge to one solution type (r7, r8, r11, r12). Convergence across runs can hold once hyperparameters are fixed in some regimes.
relationships.display_finding: Nearly all seeds selected one solution type within each tested asymmetric-initialization or extreme-width setting.
